Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), and in my absence on Monday, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) asked the following question:
By what authority is the United States air force forbidding Canadian civilians employed by them at Newfoundland bases to participate in Canadian political activities, as reported in the Sunday Herald, St. John's. Newfoundland, under date of July 1, 1956? Is this not an improper interference with the rights of Canadian citizens by a foreign power?
Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply to that question, which will no doubt be also of interest to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill).
The Department of External Affairs has made inquiries and has learned that the United States northeast air command, on its own initiative, sent a letter to its Canadian
67509-360i
employees on May 12, 1956, informing them that the provisions of the Canadian Civil Service Act regarding participation of civil servants in federal and provincial elections would be applied in principle to Canadian civilian employees of northeast air command.
The government is satisfied that the action of northeast air command, although inappropriate, was well-intentioned. After discussion between the United States and Canadian authorities, it was decided that northeast air command would rescind the instruction to Canadian employees regarding political activities.

Mr. Speaker, with reference to the question asked on Tuesday, July 3, by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) regarding the C.B.C. television series "This is Ottawa", I am informed by the C.B.C. that the purpose of the series was to provide a visual .impression of some of the varied aspects of Ottawa in its role as the national capital. Having regard to the limited number of program periods available, six periods of one-half hour each, it could not be considered and, in fact, was not planned as an historical review or a definitive documentary of the city of Ottawa.
The six programs are intended to deal with six different aspects of Ottawa as the national capital, an introduction to the national capital, Ottawa as an historic centre, as a diplomatic centre, as a centre of government research, as a cultural centre and


as the home of parliament. I am informed that those connected with the planning and production of the series experienced great difficulty in resolving the multitude of choices available in a city such as Ottawa and that programming and technical considerations as well as the convenience of the persons associated with each program of necessity had to be taken into account in choosing the locale to be related to the program.
I am informed that it was a matter of regret to the planners of this particular series that the mayor of Ottawa was unable, owing to a conflicting commitment, to accept an invitation to participate in the first program of the series dealing with the introduction to the national capital. I am further informed that limitations on the length of the series together with program and technical considerations made it impossible to include all the outstanding national sites such as Rideau Hall and Earnscliffe that the planner would have liked to include had not such limitations prevailed.

Before we proceed again with the estimates of the civil service commission, Mr. Chairman, I should like to correct the information I gave to the hon. member for Oxford yesterday concerning an item in the public accounts concerning a sum of $11,880, paid to Mr. A. M. Laidlaw for secretarial services. I then informed him that this amount of $11,880 comprised secretarial services and the payment of salary of his secretary. I now find that the sum comprises only the total amount of fees at the rate of $60 per day paid to Mr. Laidlaw for his services as secretary to the Ilsley commission for the financial year 1954-55. I might add that the commission has not hired the services of a counsel and Mr. Laidlaw also gives advice to the commission as counsel. I would think that the fee paid to him is quite reasonable on these assumptions.
While I am giving this information, I should like also to answer a question asked of me by the hon. member for Royal concerning notices which were issued by the civil service commission in which he found that the salaries offered for the two positions were not, in his estimation, justified. In other words, one of the salaries appeared to be too high in view of the qualifications that were required, and in the other case the salary was much lower than, in his estimation, it should have been. At the same time, he asked me whether there was a co-ordination agency of some kind in the civil service commission to deal with the different salaries paid for different positions in the different departments of government.
I am now informed that the civil service commission is responsible for co-ordinating the salaries of the different positions as between departments, and is responsible for assuring that the salaries paid throughout the service are equitable and uniform, based upon the duties and responsibilities of the positions involved. In this case the technical position advertised was that of geological

Supply-Secretary of State lapidary technician, competition No. 56-378, and that is a supervisory position. The qualifications require supervisory ability. The appointee must be skilled in the particular activity and make thin sections of the most difficult type including radioactive ores; he must direct and supervise the preparation of ores and rocks for study under reflected light; check thin sections under a miscros-cope; improve, and develop new techniques; consult with and give advice to members of the scientific staff. The qualifications, as a result, require a number of years of experience in this or related work and evidence of ability to perform the highly specialized work involved.
In the other case, the position advertised was that of a labour legislation analyst. In this case it is a junior position on the technical staff and it is indicated that the duties of the appointee are to note criticisms, to summarize legislative decisions; to prepare reports and correspondence and articles. The incumbent of this position is not required to exercise supervision and no prior experience is required. The position calls for those who have specialized in particular academic fields, and for those who have some knowledge of labour legislation and labour problems. In other words, it may be true that, in spite of the fact that one has to be a graduate of a university and gets a smaller salary, he has to accomplish minor functions, while in the case of this geological technician, although there is no need for graduation from a university but simply an elementary school education, he has to have highly technical qualifications, which justifies the fact there is a higher salary offered.

speechtext:
Before the item carries, I have an observation to which I feel the minister should give some thought, with respect to an item on page 167, office stationery, supplies and equipment. I note that for the ensuing year the expenditure on office stationery, supplies and equipment is to be $98,000, which is a decrease of $12,000 from last year. I am very happy to see that consideration is being given to decreasing the expenditures on stationery. I raise the question because frequently we receive through the mail certain envelopes which I am sure are quite costly, much more so than the smaller ones.
I hold in my hand a large brown envelope addressed to Mr. Ernest G. Hansell, M.P., Box 417, Vulcan, Alberta. The postal date on it is 30,11,55, which would be the 30th day of the 11th month, which would be November, 1955. In the envelope sent out by the civil service commission there were three paltry sheets. It would have been much simpler to

have folded these sheets and put them in a much smaller envelope. I am satisfied that these envelopes cost a great deal more than ones one-third the size. I make this statement because this is not a single instance. I have another envelope in my hand which is postmarked the same date, 30,11,55, and addressed to the same gentleman. It contains four sheets of paper which indicate that certain civil service positions are vacant, and which we would ask the people of Canada to apply for so that the positions would be adequately looked after. I am satisfied that all hon. members get these envelopes from time to time. I have another one postmarked 5,12,55, which is the fifth day of December, 1955. In this instance the envelope contains four sheets.
In this morning's mail I received an envelope addressed to myself dated the 4th day of this month. It is another large envelope. I might say that in between times we have received many others as well. I am just picking these out because I was able to lay my hands on them. In this particular envelope there is an advertisement for a particular job with respect to engineers and architects. It applies to only one particular position. I realize that we do have to spend money to send these advertisements all over the country, but I am wondering whether we have reached the same stage in this country that the United States of America found itself in just a short time ago when they found it necessary to set up the Hoover commission to examine into the paper work that was being done in that country. I feel that the department of the Secretary of State is at least showing good business sense by reducing the expenditures on the paper work that it has to do. I am not singling out this particular department by bringing this to the attention of the government, but it is not an uncommon thing to find that we are so much bound up by red tape in reports of different kinds that we are spending many times more than we should necessarily spend on paper work. I am satisfied that this in itself could well develop into a fine patronage program. I am also satisfied that that is probably not so in the minister's department because the expenditure involved in this department is so small that it would not lend itself greatly to that purpose. I would ask that not only his department but every department of government examine more closely into expenditures in so far as paper work is concerned and see whether or not it would be desirous to set up not a commission but an inquiry board or a firm that makes it its business to examine into better methods of administering in order to do away with the colossal expenditure on paper in this country. The paper industry is an important one in

Canada; it is an important industry in my riding. I do not think, however, it should necessarily be subsidized by the Canadian people when we find there are so many countries desirous of obtaining paper.
I might just illustrate to the minister the fact that industry does have this same difficulty and that it is recognized from time to time. I understand there was a certain firm in the United States that examined into its paper work. In the railway committee this year I inquired of Donald Gordon if we were doing anything in this respect in the railway business and he indicated to me the railway had given it some thought and not only that but they had revised their filing system at the suggestion of experts. Perhaps this question should be examined to see if any improvement could be made in the government.
The government of the United States is the only one that is carrying out this type of work, to the best of my knowledge. They found, for instance, that for each federal government employee they issued 25,000 pieces of paper per year. They compared that with certain industries and 1 must admit some of the industries were worse than the government in this respect. One industry issued 34,000 pieces of paper per employee per year, another one issued 56,000 and a third issued 64,000. Perhaps we do not issue too many pieces of paper per employee per year in the government but I do say we are spending too much money for paper work when we continue to send out bulletins in envelopes of this size.

Mr. Chairman, about the civil service commission I wish to make a few brief comments, and I shall also take the liberty of addressing one or two questions to the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard).
If I remember well, in September of last year, I think, Mr. Bland, the then chairman of the civil service commission, retired and was replaced by Mr. Nelson, the present incumbent, who, I am told, has all the qualifications and knowledge required for such a high post. He is being assisted by a compatriot of mine from the province of Quebec, Mr. Alexandre Boudreau, also a member of the commission. In view of the importance of this organization, I wonder whether or not the department intends to fill
Supply-Secretary of State as soon as possible the vacancy created by the retirement of Mr. Bland.
I understand that Messrs. Boudreau and Nelson are not on too friendly terms, with consequent inconvenience in the first place to themselves, and perhaps more particularly to the commission itself.
As things now stand at the civil service commission, I sense a danger, because those who have to deal with the various commissioners must of necessity meet them individually, since they are not together, and the danger I sense is that we are human as are also members of the commission, and because the party now in power is so mighty, numerically, we can well fear that pressures be exerted individually on the commissioners in favour of some applicant who has taken part in competition for any position in the civil service.
I am also informed that, since Easter 1951, there has not been a full meeting of the commission. I am going to repeat this, as the hon. Secretary of State's attention was directed elsewhere. As I said, I am informed -and have every reason to believe that the information is reliable-that the commission has not held a plenary sitting since Easter 1951; I mean that there has been no recorded official meeting attended by the secretary of the commission.
I submit these few remarks to the hon. Secretary of State, because I trust he will give the matter his best attention and will correct this anomaly which, to my mind, is deplorable and should not be.
As to the appointment of the third commissioner, I think, if I remember rightly, that it was the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) who, last year, suggested the appointment of a woman commissioner. Nobody objected to this suggestion, and I believe that the government tried, by various means, to find a woman who would accept this appointment.
However, may I be permitted to submit to the house that this commission cannot be efficient unless it is fully staffed at the executive level, unless all its members are present, unless they meet periodically and unless proper records are kept of the proceedings at their meetings. Should the government experience any difficulty in finding a woman to fill the post now vacant within the commission, I suggest that this appointment be made in any event without further delay, in the interests of the commission, to begin with, and of all its employees.

I have nothing more to add on this point, Mr. Chairman. I have directed these remarks to the Secretary of State who will no doubt take them into serious consideration.
Before concluding, I would like to ask whether it would not be possible-this is a mere suggestion-to bring under the civil service commission all the stenographers at present employed in the House of Commons. Everybody knows that, for the last few years, House of Commons stenographers are employed, just as we are, for the best part of the year. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to
answer briefly some of the points raised by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne).
He raised a number of them. If I remember rightly he began by referring to the allegedly strained relations which exist-or so he was told-between the present two members of the commission, Messrs. Nelson and Alexandre Boudreau.
I must say that, since July 1, 1954, that is to say from the time I was first called upon as a cabinet minister to concern myself more directly with the work of the commission,
I have had no occasion to observe that such a state of affairs did, in fact, exist. I am obviously not in a position to say whether there are any personal differences between them that could justify such a statement. However, as far as I am concerned, I have always found among them a desire to cooperate, and I had on various occasions the opportunity of seeing them together and of working with them. I have always been on excellent terms with the members of the commission.
The hon. member also mentioned the vacancy that has existed since the retirement of Mr. Bland, the former chairman of the commission.
Indeed, it is important that the commission be at its full establishment although two members constitute a quorum for its sittings. Besides, that is a wish which I expressed
[Mr. Dufresne.l

myself on various occasions, a wish that I would like to implement at the earliest possible moment. I may add that that is a position the government will have to take in due course and that, when a decision is made, I shall announce it to the house. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has already indicated, in January, that the government intended to appoint a lady to fill the position of third commissioner. I feel confident that the government will make this appointment within a few months. We shall then have a full commission that will be able to carry out its work more efficiently.
The hon. member for Quebec West also stated that the commission or the commissioners had not met formally, so to speak, since 1951. That may be because of the fact that the commissioners, who were in the habit of keeping minutes of their meetings, decided to do without these minutes for reasons best known to themselves, which they however explained to me, and also for reasons of economy. They thought it advisable to act on that decision but they still keep, I am sure, a rather complete summary of their meetings. I must also point out to my hon. friend that they meet as soon as a problem arises and as often as is warranted by circumstances. Moreover, there is no doubt that they call on each other, that they see each other, and work together, even though this coming together does not take the form of an official meeting.
As for the last suggestion of my hon. friend concerning the stenographers of the House of Commons, I believe that problem is the sole concern of the House of Commons itself. That would more properly come under the estimates of the Speaker of this house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would not want to leave the minister under the impression that relations are strained between Mr. Nelson and Mr. Boudreau. Besides, I did not make that statement. I am sure the minister understood that. I merely reported what has been told to me and I have no doubt that my information is correct, but I repeat that I did not make that statement myself.
However, Mr. Chairman, I feel that the members of the commission hold an important position, one which should require their presence twelve months a year.
Far be it from me to criticize the only French-speaking member of the commission, Mr. Alexandre Boudreau, whose ability is

fully recognized. However I know that, when he was sent on a special mission to Cambodia, Mr. Boudreau had to be away nearly a whole year, I believe. Unfortunately he was not replaced during his absence, and it might be interesting to know who took over the work and duties assigned to him.
The minister told us that, on the basis of a statement of the prime minister, he was confident that, perhaps within the next few months, a woman would be appointed a member of the civil service commission. I hope that it will be possible to bring this about very shortly, within a few weeks at the very utmost, since I feel that it is absolutely essential that this vacancy be filled at the earliest possible moment. I would still like to know, however, if the minister has enough information at this time to tell us whether this new woman member of the commission will be chosen from among the present personnel of this body, and if she has shown herself to be competent in this regard.
The minister also referred to what I have called official meetings of the commission. He told us that, according to the information at his disposal, the course taken had been chosen for reasons of economy. I frankly believe that whoever gave him that information is quite irresponsible. To my mind it is not possible to save any money by refusing to have the secretary present at these official meetings of the commission. I will even go so far as to suggest that these meetings should be held periodically.
As to the stenographers of the House of Commons, whom I mentioned just now, I thank the hon. minister for his information. They are, no doubt, under the jurisdiction of the house itself, and I shall be pleased to raise the point during the discussion concerning the Speaker's estimates.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is one
aspect of the work of the civil service commission about which I should like to say a few words. I am rather amused when I hear arguments put forth from time to time by various members of the house in which they hurl such charges as patronage and so on at the government so far as appointments to the civil service are concerned. I think I can say fairly honestly that in the province of British Columbia a federal civil service position is one of the lowliest of positions to which a wage earner can aspire. It is only those people who have a socal consciousness, who are willing to put aside their selfish interests, who are willing to serve the community rather than acquire any money for themselves, who are willing to work for the federal government.
As an aside, I should like to recommend to the civil service commission that an application for a position with the federal government that is accompanied by a recommendation from the local member of parliament

Supply-Secretary of State should be automatically ruled out because in my opinion any would-be civil servant who does not hold the necessary qualifications for the position and needs the support of a local politician should be automatically disqualified.
I am not one to condone waste on the part of any department of the government, and that also includes the civil service. Like the hon. member for New Westminster, who has already spoken, I was a little surprised this morning when I received this huge, impressive looking envelope containing only three or four sheets of paper all of which could have been enclosed quite adequately in a much smaller envelope or might not even have needed an envelope at all but only my name on the outside of the folder.
I want to speak about one aspect of the civil service commission that has for some time now, at least to those of us in the west, seemed most unrealistic, and that is its failure to recognize the salaries that are available to men of ability with qualifications in fields other than the civil service. Just as one example, I hold in my hand an advertisement by the civil service commission asking for applicants for the position of superintendent of schools at Fort Smith in the Northwest Territories. The salary offered is $5,330 to $5,970 per annum. I have in my other hand a copy of the latest issue of the B. C. Teacher wherein they publish the salary scales obtaining for the province of British Columbia. I see that the city of Vancouver offers a teacher with similar qualifications, but without having to assume any responsibility of supervision or superintending whatsoever, a salary as high as $6,200 a year. New Westminster offers $5,900 a year. In Burnaby they are offered a possible $6,050 a year. I could go on further. In West Vancouver they are offering $6,200 a year. This is for the ordinary classroom teacher. The civil service commission attempts to obtain a superintendent of schools at $5,330. We can well imagine what sort of applicant they are likely to get. I see that the commission itself recognizes the utter ridiculousness of the situation because under the qualifications they call for a provincial first-class teaching certificate. In other words, the civil service commission is quite prepared to send a man who has a first-class teacher's certificate up into that part of Canada to be a superintendent of schools and to be superior to the principals there who may have their Bachelor's degree, their Master's degree or possibly even their Doctor's degree and are likely to know one hundred times as much about the profession as does the so-called federal civil servant, the superintendent of schools.

I have another circular here in which an assistant superintendant of schools at Fort Smith is called for at a salary of $4,750 a year. Some of our primary teachers in western Canada receive that salary without any degree whatsoever. Then I have another one here calling for a current affairs officer for the Department of National Defence, a most responsible position, where a man is supposed to be responsible for the supplying of reliable information for the education of members of our armed services-adults-in Canada. They call for graduation from a university, majoring in history, economics or geography. They call for a number of years' experience in the writing of articles and the editing of manuscripts. They are offering the magnificent sum of $4,750 which again, I submit, is most unrealistic.
Economists are called for by the Department of Agriculture. In information circular No. 56-18 the terms of employment are given. Salaries begin at $3,300 per annum. Surely any economist who is willing to work for $3,300 a year must be either completely self-effacing or a worthless fellow who has been thrown into the discard heap by all the other possible employers throughout Canada.
Then we have an advertisement-and I find this advertisement all the time; I receive one of them almost every week-calling for a librarian, at a salary of $3,030. They call for a Bachelor's degree in library science. Anyone with a Bachelor's degree in library science can go to almost any one of our urban school boards and receive a salary that is much in excess of that.
Then in order to educate the members of the Canadian armed forces, they call for a staff training officer at Halifax, Toronto, Ottawa, Winnipeg, Vancouver. There is one position, grade 3, with the salary of $4,360. The qualifications are graduation from a university of recognized standing; responsible work experience, part of which must have been in a supervisory capacity; ability to organize, conduct and develop courses of instruction and group discussion; ability to deal with senior officers. I could go on.
I see here that electrical engineers are called for and are being offered $6,840 per annum whereas I understand that an electrical engineer worth his salt is worth $18,000 in private industry any day. However, I think this is one of the best of them all. They call for customs excise officers in Quebec-where it may be a good salary; I do not now-and also in British Columbia at a salary of $215 a month.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It is not any better in Quebec than it is any place else.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
It is not a decent salary even in the province of Quebec; thank you. No decent, self-respecting individual who has a family to look after is going to consider a salary of $215 a month. You cannot maintain a household these days on that salary. I am not surprised when we find complaints against the manner of service offered by the civil servants of Canada when that is what the commission thinks is an adequate remuneration.
Then they call for information and records engineers and offer a salary up to $4,620 a year. Many people completely unskilled in any profession at all in western Canada earn that much in a year. Another position advertised is that of hospital nursing assistant. The salary offered is $1,920 a year. For ward clerks they offer $1,800 a year. A waitress working in any cafe in eastern Canada, if she includes the tips she gets, would not consider looking at a salary like that. It used to be an honour throughout Canada to be an employee of the government of Canada. It is no longer so today. I realize the civil service commission is not entirely to blame but I do feel in the relationships the civil service commission's recommendations play a very important part.
Here I find the Canadian pension commission is asking for doctors for $6,700 a year. I doubt very much whether you can find an honest, reputable doctor in Canada who will admit that he earns only $6,700 a year. We must remember one thing in connection with these young people. When they apply for these positions, we at least hope that they intend to make a lifetime career in the public service. When we offer a doctor $6,700 a year I submit that we are not inviting him in any way shape or form to make the public service a career. I see lawyers being called for by the department of the Minister of Justice and being offered $5,700 a year. An LL.B. degree from a university is not sufficient; oh, no. They must have been admitted to the bar. They must have had experience. Yet they are being offered less than $500 a month. Miners in British Columbia earn that kind of money. You do not need a university degree or you do not need to be admitted to the bar and to have served a period of apprenticeship to merit that type of salary.
I see that a lecturer in civil engineering is called for. He has not only to be a civil engineer but he must be able to lecture in civil engineering. He is being offered less than $400 a month; the salary offered is $4,620 a year. Then I see that they are asking for a lecturer in economics. Not only must he be an able economist himself but he must be able to lecture to others in
67509-361J
Supply-Secretary of State economics. The salary offered is $4,620 a year. I have others here. I see that a dental surgeon is being called for. I should not say that one is being called for. I see there are vacancies at Quebec city, Moose Factory, Sioux Lookout, North Battleford, Prince Albert, Regina, Calgary, Prince Rupert, Chilliwack, Vancouver, Fort Smith and Aklavik. This shows what is happening as a result of the unrealistic attitude taken by the civil service commission. They need not one dental surgeon but they have vacancies in six different places in Canada at the same time.
Now, this is one particular occupation about which I have had a lot of complaints. The Indians of Canada are not receiving the dental care with which the minister would like to supply them and the main reason, I am informed, is the inadequacy of the salaries being offered to dental surgeons. We see evidence of that when they list vacancies at 12 different places in Canada at one and the same time. The commission is offering a salary of $6,300 a year. I realize that since the time some of these figures I have read into the records were published there has been an increase for most of the civil servants in Canada, if not all. However, I am confident that even with the increase the relative position of these people as opposed to those in private enterprise or those who enlist for service in municipal and other governmental institutions in Canada will show that the federal service is becoming a beggar's job indeed. It is only the loyalty of those people that causes them to continue to serve.
There is one more advertisement I want to put on the record and it is for a lecturer in chemistry at the Royal Military College, Kingston. He is offered the magnificent sum of $4,950 per annum. It is not surprising, Mr. Chairman, that so many of these forms give evidence of the desperate situation in which the civil service commission finds itself. These advertisements list not only the salary but the benefits as well. They make a big noise about the other benefits the servant will receive, such as three weeks' annual holidays; sick leave; contributory superannuation; optional hospital and medical insurance plan and low cost term insurance. These things are not news to the average young man walking into the post office in New Westminster. Since we have no post office in Burnaby, I cannot mention that.
A young man walks in and reads these advertisements. He sees all these other benefits, but he finds nothing exceptional in them. Out west these things are no longer mentioned in advertisements for employees. They are accepted as the natural benefits that employees

Supply-Secretary of State receive. Almost anyone working for a worthwhile organization, anyone belonging to a union, enjoys these benefits and more than those listed here. I realize there may be places where they are an added lure with which to get the innocent into the civil service. However, I feel the time is long overdue in Canada when we must once again make the remuneration of civil servants such that other people in Canada will want to apply for a position in the civil service. This should be an occupation that is looked upon, not with pity, but in a manner that would foster in the young people of Canada a desire to serve the community at large in the knowledge that if they did serve the community at large they would be well rewarded or rewarded at least as well as the average person who does not work for the community at large but in his own more immediate interest.

speechtext:
I should like to say a few words about the civil service commission. Like my friend the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, I too studied the civil service notices that have been issued for various competitions. It seems to me that the civil service commission is tending to defeat its own ends in many ways. I agree with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that the salaries offered are small when

compared with the qualifications that are required. The argument has been put forward that civil service salaries are small in comparison with industrial salaries because of the security factor. This argument does not hold up, because so far as I can see today the civil servant does not have any more security than he would have in industrial life.
I know of two gentlemen in my own riding who were civil servants before confederation. In accordance with the terms of union, they were taken into the federal civil service, but their positions were washed out. They were operators of a bait depot. The department leased the bait depots to private interests and those jobs were washed out. I believe these people had had 10 years' service and had been looking forward to superannuation, but the job disappeared and their security disappeared along with it. The security factor, therefore, is not an argument in favour of low salaries.
The other thing I should like to point out is that the qualifications that are listed often make such great demands that it narrows the number of people who apply. There are a good many people who are capable, who are honest people and who are modest. They read these qualifications and say, "Well, I am not good enough for that, so I will not apply." They do not apply because they do not feel they have the qualifications listed and it is no use for them to do so. What happens then? Some person who is not nearly so modest will apply, and when the competition is run you get a number of people who are, perhaps, inferior to the people who would have applied if the qualifications listed had not made such high demands.
The other point that occurs to me in connection with this problem is that the application forms for civil service positions require almost a person's biography. He has to list all his previous jobs for the last 10 years and I believe that, too, defeats the purpose the commission had in mind because very often the applicant is a jack-of-all-trades. He has certain qualities which do not enable him to keep the job he has, so he flits from one job to another. He may fill out the whole back of the sheet with the 10 or 12 different positions that he has had within the past 10 years, and he gets credit for that and also for his experience, and very often it is the wrong kind of experience that he gets credit for. I would suggest that the commission revise these forms and also the requirements they ask for when they advertise these positions.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is another matter that I should like to bring before the civil service commission that slipped my mind when I was speaking a few minutes ago. speechtext:
In the past two years, at the request of some members of the committee, the estimates of the dominion coal board were taken up first. Although the matter of the estimates of the dominion coal board is still very important, I would suggest that we follow the items as printed in the book this year.
The year 1955, with a mineral production figure close to $1,800 million has proven a new all-time record year for Canada. In the last few years the estimates of total production have all fallen short and proven to 

be on the low side, and the $2 billion mark at which the industry has been aiming and hoped to reach by 1960 will probably be reached this year.
Numerous new mining properties with good production potential continue to emerge right across Canada. At the turn of the year, no less than 60 mine shafts were being sunk in Canada on properties in advanced stage of exploration or development. Of particular significance is Canada's fast increasing production of iron ore, petroleum and uranium. Our iron ore production jumped spectacularly from 7-3 million tons in 1954 to 17-3 million tons in 1955. Indications are that the production of iron ore in 1956 will be greatly increased.
The search for uranium ores and the proving up of properties still held the spotlight in 1955. Special contracts signed with the Eldorado Mining and Refining Company on the closing date of March 31 last, as well as letters of intent to sign contracts, involve a total of over $700 million for the purchase of uranium precipitates. As these contracts call for delivery before March 31, 1962, we may well expect increasingly high production figures.
Petroleum still topped the list in Canada in 1955, with a production figure of over $300 million, an increase of $59 million over the 1954 production. Most of the petroleum output is from Alberta, but it is noteworthy indeed that both Manitoba and Saskatchewan doubled their production in 1955 over the previous year.
The search for and the development of minerals involves a very high element of risk, and the work of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is intended, by research and by the development of new methods and techniques and by improved mapping, to reduce as far as possible that element of risk. The mineral industry, by its production of new wealth, provides a very important stimulus to the whole economy of the nation. The benefits of this production of new wealth extend right into every household in Canada. Because of the hardships and the high element of risk involved, the industry attracts people who have the qualities of adventure, persistence and resourcefulness. I am pleased to state that the relationship between the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the mineral industry has been excellent.
Following our custom of recent years, the department has prepared another summary of activities for the year 1955, which is in the hands of hon. members, as is our annual report. I trust that this summary of activities

has proven useful, and I would invite comments from hon. members. Someone usually asks the cost of the production of the summary. I am told it cost $240 to produce it this year.
I should like for a few minutes to review the organization and the work of the various branches of the department and the divisions of those branches, as related to the amounts of money requested in the estimates for this year.
The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys exists primarily to aid the growth of the mining industry in Canada and to provide the necessary surveys for exploration and development of our natural resources. It is fundamentally an investigative department, and for purposes of administration is divided into five branches as follows:
1.	Surveys and mapping branch, with a hydrographic regional office in Victoria, B.C.
2.	The geological survey of Canada, with five regional offices, namely, in Vancouver, Yellowknife, Whitehorse, Calgary and Sydney.
3.	The mines branch, with a regional fuels division in Alberta.
4.	The geographical branch.
5.	The dominion observatory in Ottawa and the dominion astrophysical observatory in Victoria, B.C., with other substations.
I should like to deal first with the surveys and mapping branch. One of the divisions of its responsibilities is air photography. Before the last war there were great stretches of country, particularly in the north, that had no maps whatever, or if they had maps they were only based on traverses along a river where a traveller had made some rough sketches. Air photography has changed this completely. Originally the flying was mainly done by the R.C.A.F., but the appropriations as now provided by this department call for contract flying of areas selected according to their greatest need for both military and civilian purposes. In the fiscal year ended March, 1956, this department expects to spend its appropriation of $1,250,000 and a supplementary estimate of $550,000 for this purpose and for the present fiscal year we are requesting $1,500,000.
In order to get maps during the war, the north was covered by a trimetrogon system of pictures which consists of one vertical and two lateral oblique photographs taken at the same time. These pictures allowed the preparation of general maps on the scale of 1 inch to 8 miles. These were satisfactory for air navigation and reconnaissance investigations of the geology and mineral deposits, but too limited in accuracy for more detailed
5, 1956	5685
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys study. Consequently, all areas that were covered in a preliminary way by trimetrogon photographs are now gradually being covered by vertical photography. Much of the flying is done at about 30,000 feet to give wider coverage with less flying than at lower levels. Lower flying will be required in some areas for greater details of topography or for special purposes. All this is arranged through an interdepartmental committee on air photography of which the deputy minister of this department is chairman. Under favourable weather conditions it will be possible to have the whole of Canada, exclusive of the Arctic islands, covered by vertical photography by the end of 1957. There will be a continuing need for further photography taken at various heights to meet special requirements, such as forest inventory, geology, power development, defence projects, flood control and others.
I come now to the geodetic survey. In order to place map sheets in their proper relationship to one another and in their proper place in reference to longitude and latitude, it is necessary that a triangulation net of points be fixed in reference to one another. Also, in order that the surveyed altitude of various points may have true relations to one another and to the datum at sea level, their elevations must be determined with precision. Formerly, in fixing triangulation points, the geodetic survey built signalling towers and, by a rather slow process of observing angles between stations, built up a triangulation net in which all points of observations were accurately determined. Following the war this older method was replaced, in the north particularly, by modern electronic methods. By these it is possible to measure lines 300 miles in length with a precision of 20 feet.
This work by the geodetic survey has been done in conjunction with the R.C.A.F., and has become a model for geodetic work for all undeveloped parts of the world. It has allowed us in a few years to extend a triangulation net for accurate mapping from southern Manitoba to the Arctic and across the Arctic islands to Labrador where it will be joined to a net from the St. Lawrence area. This work has already occupied five field seasons, and several more will be required to complete it. Necessarily, expenditures for such surveys are heavy, but in relation to former slower and more laborious methods the unit cost per square mile is very much less. In fact, the work that is being done would be impossible by the older methods owing to the remoteness and isolation of most of the areas that are now being covered.
For the work of the geodetic survey for the coming year we are asking for $567,786, an

The geodetic survey has 52 permanent employees of which the technical staff, highly skilled in surveying methods and in mathematics, numbers 30. The chief of this division is also the head of the Canadian section of the international boundary commission which is responsible for the surveying and maintenance of all international boundary lines and monuments. For this fiscal year it is estimated that $58,060 will be needed for this purpose, a decrease of $3,021 from the previous year.
Next I will deal with the topographical survey branch. The actual physical features shown on our maps by contour lines result from the work of the topographical survey. This division uses the precise elevations and the fixed points established by the geodetic survey.
In the preparation of maps, air photographs are used extensively. During and since the war great progress has been made in using various types of plotting instruments to transfer information from air photographs to a map surface.
The work of the topographer in secondary triangulation and in obtaining field data has been greatly speeded up by the use of helicopters. These are used most effectively in country relatively free of timber. They have also proven very efficient in extensive mapping we have done in the Yukon, in the Northwest Territories and in Labrador. In fact, their use is essential if map making is to keep pace with the demands of the mineral industry and for other purposes. The use of helicopters with supporting aircraft is very expensive, but the unit cost per square mile has been greatly reduced by the greater amount of country covered in one season. There has been as much as a tenfold increase for a single field party over older methods and better results are obtained. For the topographical survey for the present fiscal year we are asking for $1,690,232, a decrease of $27,833 from the previous year.
The next division is legal surveys and aeronautical charts. Legal surveys are necessary for land subdivision and are carried out under the direction of the surveyor general. They are done by this department as a service to other departments such as northern affairs and national resources and for the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. Provincial boundary surveys are carried out in conjunction with the various provinces. Necessarily, legal surveys need to be done with accuracy and by well qualified land surveyors. We have found difficulty in maintaining an adequate staff to meet the demands that are being made on us because there is a great attraction for this
[Mr. Prudham.l

type of surveyor in private enterprise owing to Canada's rapid expansion.
This division is also responsible for the production of Canadian aeronautical charts according to a world standard set by international agreement, and it co-operates with the Department of Transport in the publication of the Canada Air Pilot.
The division also prepares descriptions of the electoral districts of Canada according to the Representation Act and issues the electoral maps. For the provincial and territorial boundary surveys we are asking for $50,725 for this fiscal year, a decrease of $3,725 from the previous year.
The next division is the Canadian hydrographic service. Our hydrographic service performs a very important function in charting our coasts and our inland waters, measuring tidal currents and levels, and issuing charts and tables for shipping. We have three major vessels on the Pacific coast and four on the eastern coast. Also, for the past several years we have chartered two boats for northern work on the east coast, and we have other smaller boats on inland waters, including the great lakes and Great Slave lake. In fact, we use about sixteen boats in all in our work in making soundings for charts. Here again, newer sonic methods are replacing older techniques and fixation of points is being done electronically rather than by direct shore observation. Not only have such methods greatly increased the amount of work one ship can do in a season, but this work can be done out of the sight of land in such areas as the gulf of St. Lawrence and in weather when visibility is low. For our work in the north we are building a modern ship specially designed for Arctic work. It was launched two or three weeks ago and is expected to be commissioned this autumn. This vessel the Baffin will cost about $4 million and will be equipped, as I have said, with the very latest implements and also will be served by helicopters.
For the work of the hydrographic service we are asking $3,478,652 for this fiscal year. This is a decrease of $1,023,484 from the previous year, largely resulting from less payments on the construction of our new ship, the Baffin.

In the surveys and mapping branch we maintain a division for the compilation and printing of maps. This means we have a drafting staff, and much photographic and other equipment necessary for this work. Last year we distributed about one million maps. We have eight map-printing presses,

They also serve on an interdepartmental committee with officials of the Department of Finance and National Revenue in relation to mine taxation problems.
Radioactivity Division:
In the radioactivity division the work is again one of the methods of processing ores, but it is largely of a chemical nature since leaching is commonly used in the treatment of radioactive minerals. The new developments in the lake Athabaska area in Saskatchewan and in the Blind river and Bancroft areas in Ontario have been spectacular in the varieties of ore bodies discovered and in the tonnages disclosed. For all these properties, milling and recovery practices have had to be established. The work of this division has contributed greatly to the success in making Canada a very important producer of uranium, especially in the work of developing methods of producing metal from low grade ore.
For mineral resources investigations, research, and acquisition of new equipment for the whole of the mines branch, we are asking $3,205,355. This is a decrease of $75,996 from the previous year.
Geographical Branch:
The geographical branch, established in 1947, carries out a number of projects in northern Canada directly related to air photo interpretation of terrain. Key areas are selected for study, and from the interpretations made from air photographs of these it is possible to make interpretations in other areas. This work is mainly for the joint intelligence bureau of national defence.
Studies of various cities are being made for the civil defence division of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Also a compilation is made of the information relating to the distribution of ice conditions in northern Canada and in the gulf of St. Lawrence. This information is valuable to the Department of Transport in relation to navigation.
Work on the atlas of Canada has been under way for a number of years. I believe the last time I stood before this committee I thought that it would be completed this year, but that has not been possible. We have made considerable progress, but because of the priority of other projects the work on the atlas has lagged somewhat.

Dominion Observatories:
The dominion observatories in Ottawa and Victoria, B.C., are maintained by this department. Observations of stars are essential to the maintenance of a time service. This is given with a precision that is essential for longitude determination, as well as public use. The investigations carried out by two field stations at Meanook and Newbrook in northern Alberta are in relation to the rate of meteor travel in the high atmosphere. This is a subject of interest to national defence in connection with the use of high velocity projectiles. We maintain a terrestrial magnetism section at Ottawa, and through this the declination of the compass is given to our other surveys for each map sheet issued. The information collected by this section is of practical value in making aero-magnetic maps for airborne magnetometers such as are in use by our geological survey and by private interests.
Magnetic stations are maintained for observations at Agincourt, Ontario, Meanook, Alberta; Baker lake and Resolute bay, Northwest Territories. We also continue to carry out observations of gravity, and the force of gravity at many points in Canada has been determined. This is of practical application in many ways, one of which is in pipe-line construction. This is of great value as basic information in making gravity maps used as an aid to prospecting.
Seismic records are kept at the dominion observatory at Ottawa and in a more recently established station at our Victoria observatory. In all, we have 12 seismic recording stations from Halifax to the west coast.
The work of the astrophysical observatory in Victoria is concerned primarily with scientific studies relating to the composition and character of the stars, planets and interstellar materials and the application of the results to terrestrial physics.
For the dominion observatories we are asking for $814,250, an increase of $75,727 over the previous year. This increase is largely connected with our activities for the geophysical year during which world-wide observations by many countries will be correlated. The basic studies for the geophysical year are related to the influence of the sun on the upper atmosphere and hence our

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys studies are primarily related to this objective. However magnetic observations are very important because of the fact that the north magnetic pole is in Canadian territory and our scientists will have an important part in these investigations.
The Explosives Act is administered by this department, which deals with the licensing, handling and storage of explosives, of which 132,824,000 pounds were produced for commercial purposes in Canada in 1955. The expenditures for this, including a small testing laboratory maintained in Ottawa, are expected to be $107,865 for this fiscal year, an increase of $9,525. A new explosives factory at Seven Islands is now in operation and another factory is under construction at North Bay, and these will involve additional inspection services.
This department, as I have said, administers the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act which was extended by parliament recently at the same rate for the years 1957 and 1958. As hon. members are aware, the amount paid is based on a formula in relation to the cost of producing an ounce of gold. Our estimated expenditures for this fiscal year are $16,431,915, exclusive of the emergency gold mining assistance. This compares with our estimate of $17,263,091 for the previous year, a decrease of $831,176.
At present the permanent staff of our department numbers 1,929, of whom 1,754 are in Ottawa. It is housed in many buildings widely scattered in this city. This for many years has impeded efficiency and caused difficulties in administration. Plans are under way for the construction of permanent buildings to house the larger part of our staff in the vicinity of our Booth street buildings now occupied by the mines branch. A chemical and radioactivity laboratory is now under construction. A geological survey building and an administration building are planned for early construction. For these buildings, including $135,000 for improvements to the heating plant, $2,852,000 has been placed in this year's estimates of the Department of Public Works.
In the near future we wish to construct a surveys and mapping building to bring together the various surveys and map compilation and reproduction division. The cost of this whole program is expected to be of the order of $12 million to $15 million. Also, for the current year provision is being made through the Department of Public Works for $200,000 for a wharf for our hydrographic ships at Victoria, British Columbia.
This statement, Mr. Chairman, is only an outline of some of the many activities of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
[Mr. Prudham.l

Our relationships with the mining industry are cordial and on a co-operative basis. Our surveys and investigations are undertaken in consultation with provincial authorities under whose jurisdiction the mineral resources are administered. In this way duplication of effort is avoided, and provincial and federal projects are complementary to one another.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the minister for the detailed statement he has given to the committee in connection with the estimates and the administration of his department. Since it is my intention to deal very briefly, of course, with the development of the natural resources in my province of Quebec, I am sure the minister will allow me to continue my remarks in my mother tongue.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I take part in the discussion of the estimates of the Mines and Technical Surveys department in order to show briefly the great development of our natural resources, especially in the province of Quebec.
My province, I daresay, is unquestionably the province of Canada where, during these last few years, progress in that field has been the greatest, not to say the most fantastic. Boundless new areas, which a few years ago were outside civilization, have been opened up. They hold priceless wealth which is being developed for the benefit of the province where it is to be found and which provides Canada and the whole world with a practically inexhaustible source of ores of all kinds, thus contributing to our economic expansion and to Canadian prosperity. The huge mining development that has taken place in the Ungava district is unequalled in the history both of the province of Quebec and of our great country.
Several hundred million tons of iron ore have already been discovered and this ore is being mined at growing pace.
This vast territory, now opened up to civilization and international trade, has, in many ways, brought wealth to the province of Quebec.
Thanks to the excellent credit position which our province enjoys abroad, American capital, now mainly controlled by Canadians, is greatly contributing to our prosperity.
Since these important iron fields were first developed, the province of Quebec has known, and will know, ever-increasing expansion and prosperity.

Thousands of new jobs have been created, which brings a much needed security to many Canadian homes.
Factories of all kinds have been added to others already existing, and it appears that before long, considering the huge projects now under way, a territory heretofore ignored will become the Eden of a large number of Canadians.
Several new cities are going up in hitherto scarcely known areas, and will provide homes, full employment and security to thousands of our fellow citizens, whose contribution to their provinces and to their country will play a prominent part in the useful development of our territory.
New income sources, for the individuals as well as for the governments will contribute to the development, the greatness and the prosperity of Canada. Such an improved and secure income for individuals will relieve the burden weighing already too heavily upon governments, owing to the repeated requests for assistance to those affected by chronic or acute unemployment.
Governments increasing their income through the development of such natural resources, the authorities will then be in a position to divert to the welfare of the people the surpluses accumulated annually.
We can never be too thankful to divine Providence for endowing our province with such untold wealth which allows us to play towards humanity the part, the providential part, assigned to us.
The presence of this wealth in our soil is not a result of mere fate or coincidence; this wealth was placed there to insure the happiness of our people and to allow our people to make it available to others.
Research already initiated must be continued. The developments which we are given to witness at the present time must expand unceasingly for the benefit of our people.
I take this opportunity to pay a warm tribute and express sincere thanks to those who preside over the destinies of the province of Quebec and who are the fortunate ones responsible for this gigantic development of our resources.

This group is interested in an accurate recording of Canadian history of exploration and geography and the complete protection of Canada's sovereign rights. Now, I have always been interested in geography, and particularly in the history of the exploration of the Canadian Arctic. I must say the tempo of my interest was somewhat increased last year as the result of a conversation with an officer of the Royal Canadian Air Force who had been serving in the Arctic and who was himself very concerned about the maintenance of Canadian sovereignty and the apparent ignorance of certain United States army personnel concerning Canadian rights in the Arctic.
I am going to say a few words this afternoon about what I will term the forgotten expedition. Last year I placed a question on the order paper asking for a definition of the land area that is considered to be within the jurisdiction of Canada north of the mainland of this country and later, at the suggestion of certain people, I withdrew that question. As a result, apparently there was a radio news report and a constituent of mine, Dr. L. E. Borden, who was a member of the first Canadian Arctic expedition, contacted me because this report disturbed him very much indeed as it indicated there was some uncertainty on the part of this government as to our territorial rights in the Arctic and when they were established.
On investigating this situation I found there were good sound grounds for Dr. Borden's concern. In fact, on checking what books I could find and various reports and articles published by scientific societies, I found what I considered an amazing situation. I found first of all in the Canadian Geographic Journal, 1935, volume 10, an article by W. Eggleston entitled "Canada's Northernmost Island." There was no mention whatever therein of the cruise of the Neptune in 1903 and 1904 under Commander A. P. Low, which was the first Canadian Arctic expedition.
Then I found in a book published by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys an article entitled "The Canadian Arctic- 1951". While there is a brief mention of this expedition there is no mention made of Commander Low taking possession of Ellesmere, Southampton and other islands on behalf of the Dominion of Canada. I obtained a copy of the periodical Arctic, which is the journal of the Arctic Institute of North America, volume 8, No. 1, 1955, and I found there an article entitled "Northern Ellesmere Island"


by G. Hattersley Smith, and again no mention is made of Canada's first Arctic expedition although this article was written particularly to list and deal with all the expeditions to the Canadian Arctic. Then I was amazed to find in the Canadian Geographic Journal of June, 1956, an article by Andrew Taylor entitled "Our Polar Islands-The Queen Elizabeths" which again overlooks Canada's first Arctic expedition.
At any rate I was cheered later by information given to me by the minister. Knowing I was interested in this question the minister directed my attention to a book published by his department in December of last year entitled "Geographical Discovery and Exploration in the Queen Elizabeth Islands". In this booklet for the first time-and I have gone through the department's records for many years past-we find an adequate reference to the cruise of the Neptune in 1903 and 1904, and I want to acknowledge the assistance I received from the minister in this respect. I think this article was included for the first time as the result of the minister's interest in this question when the uncertainties were unfolded last year.
On page 111 I find chapter 7 dealing with Canadian expeditions, and there it says:
Early in 1903, the government of Canada decided to send a vessel "to patrol the waters of Hudson bay and those adjacent to the eastern Arctic islands". The expedition was placed under command of a geologist, A. P. Low, and the government chartered the Neptune, the "largest and most powerful ship of the Newfoundland sealing fleet", for this purpose.
Then it goes on to deal quite extensively with certain aspects of this expedition, and I must say I am very pleased to see this expedition noticed for the first time for many years in a government publication. Commander Low commanded the first Canadian expedition to the Arctic on instructions from the minister of marine of that day; I think it was Hon. Mr. Prefontaine. On his return he published a report of over 350 pages which contains a great deal of interesting information on the physical features of the Arctic islands, Eskimos, the geology of the area, the flora and fauna, the possibilities of navigation of Hudson bay for the taking of wheat from Fort Churchill, whaling, an historical summary of preceding expeditions, and his report also contains other interesting matters.
I understand there are only a few copies of this report in existence, including one that I found in the library, which obviously belonged to Captain J. E. Bernier, and one, I understand, in the possession of the department. So far as I can find there are no other records of this expedition, except four or five small leather-bound notebooks in the geological section of

the minister's department, which contain some brief and fragmentary pencilled notes by Commander Low. I want to thank the minister for having had these notebooks looked up and for informing me that they were available and that I might read them. I saw one or two interesting items in them. They are very sketchy and obviously only the remnants of Commander Low's notebooks. There is a note for September 4 to October 3, 1903:
Gears stored under coal. Burned 600 pounds coal today. Average 7-5 knots. Must be careful of our coal now half gone.
I thought that was a remarkable 24-hours steaming at 7-5 knots in those days. I noticed that on June 22, 1904, there were some notes on an illness suffered by Dr. L. E. Borden, who was the surgeon and botanist. Apparently there are no other records, diaries, proclamations, expense accounts or other information available in connection with this expedition. The Minister of Transport has very kindly had the records of the Department of Transport searched; the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources had the records of his department searched, and the dominion archivist has searched the dominion archives. So far as I know there are no records available of this expedition other than the ones I have mentioned.
Before proceeding I wish to quote briefly from Commander Low's report of his expedition, "The Cruise of the Neptune, 1903-04", which is prefaced by some remarks by Hon. Raymond Prefontaine, K.C., minister of marine and fisheries. This is dated at Ottawa, September 8, 1905. It says in part:
I have great pleasure in calling attention to the valuable work of the scientific staff of the expedition. Dr. L. E. Borden, by his skill and attention, kept everybody in a good general state of health, and in addition rendered great assistance in the collection of specimens and data relating to ethnology, botany and zoology.
He goes on to give the order in council giving authority for the expedition, and so on. I would just like to say a word or two about Dr. L. E. Borden, who happens to be a personal friend, and I know he also is a long-time personal friend of our chairman, who I am sure would support any complimentary remarks I have to make about Dr. Borden.
