Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys commenced the practice of medicine. He held the rank of major in the first and second world wars. He represented the Nelson constituency in the provincial legislature from 1928 to 1933. He has been active in many community organizations, and has had a long-time interest in mining and prospecting organizations. I think at one time he was president of the miners' and prospectors' organization of the Kootenays. He is respected and highly thought of by all who know him and, I must say, particularly by the veterans he served continuously from 1914 until 1947, when he retired from active practice.
Dr. Borden was present when Commander Low took possession of Ellesmere and Southampton islands, and has copies of both proclamations, diaries, samples of Eskimo art and carvings. He is, so far as I know, the only survivor of the expedition. I am going to say at this time that I have tried to get a copy of the proclamations concerning the taking of possession of these islands in the name of the Queen and of Canada. So far as I can find out there is not a copy of those proclamations in any department of government. I think it is quite safe to say on that account that the government has lost the title deeds to the Arctic.
I understand that when Commander Low took possession of these islands-and Dr. Borden has pictures of the crew raising the flag and taking the salute-there was a copy. Commander Low wrote three copies, one for his purpose, one to be delivered to the dominion government, and one now in the possession of Dr. Borden. I am just going to put the proclamations on the record for the information of the minister and those interested in this history. This is the proclamation in connection with taking possession of the island of Southampton:
In the name of our gracious sovereign King Edward VII and on behalf of the government of Canada, I renew and take possession of this island of Southampton for the use and property of the Dominion of Canada. God save the King.
A. P. Low 23/6/04
Then he said:
Having raised the dominion ensign on the cairn and recited the above in the presence of the crew we gave three cheers for the King.
Then I have a copy of one of the three original proclamations which was given to me by Dr. Borden. This proclamation reads:
In the name of King Edward VII, and on behalf of the government of the Dominion of Canada, I have this day taken possession of the island of Ellesmereland and all the smaller islands adjoining it.
And in token of such formal possession have caused the flag of the Dominion of Canada to be
5694	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
hoisted upon the land of Ellesmereland: and have deposited a copy of this document, sealed in a metal box, in a cairn erected on the conspicuous headland of Cape Isabella.
A. P. Low,
Officer in charge of dominion expedition to Hudson bay and northward.
On board
Dominion steamship Neptune Smith sound.
11 August, 1904.
I have had some very interesting correspondence with Dr. Borden and I am going to quote briefly from a few of his letters. I might mention at this time that Dr. Borden, for health reasons, has left Nelson and now resides in Victoria. He has been there for about a year. His address is 1315 Monterey avenue, Victoria, B.C. He has this to say in writing about his personal experiences:
From my diary of August 10, 1904:-
He is quoting his own diary.
"This is truly historic ground." The next day we landed and deposited the proclamation as per A. P. Low's report on page 48, paragraph 1 of the "Cruise of the Neptune". I am probably the only living person who witnessed this ceremony of taking formal possession of Ellesmere as I also witnessed on June 23, 1904, Commander Low take formal possession of Southampton island in Hudson bay.
The time of the event of taking possession of Ellesmere which occurred to us of the expedition is of great importance and cannot well be forgotten as the midnight sun was shining in all its glory and we had just had a miraculous escape from death the day before when the Neptune struck a submerged reef.
Then in another letter he mentions some quite interesting facts. He has this to say:
As surgeon for the expedition X was asked by the government to make a report on the health of the Eskimo, especially noting tuberculosis, syphilis and cancer. As far as I know this was the first report ever submitted to the dominion government on the health of the Eskimo. I reported that I had found tuberculosis not prevalent but cases of both chest and bone; that syphilis was present but only, as far as X could find, in the tertiary stage; and as for cancer, after examining Eskimo of all ages in winter encampments and on a voyage of over 10,000 miles in summer at every port of call I never found a case and I may note that a good many years afterward I noticed in a report from a doctor at Aklavik that he had never seen a case. And just for the record may I draw your attention to the fact that Dr. Sweitzer of Lamberene in Africa reports that he has never found a case of cancer in a native.
As botanist I was supposed and did go ashore every time a boat went off to look for specimens. I have, therefore, a very particular cause to remember all landings and events that took place are still very fresh in my memory . . .
Dr. Borden was the first Canadian to botanize the Arctic on behalf of the government of Canada. Commander Low made a great contribution to our knowledge of the
[Mr. Herridge.l

Arctic as commander of this first Canadian expedition, and he also reported quite fully in his book on the possibilities for navigation in Hudson bay. Incidentally, he was also the first man to discover iron ore in Ungava.
I happened to pick that up out of a book I was checking in connection with my investigation. I wondered whether Canada had recognized the work of Commander Low, and I am glad to know that a mountain in the Rockies on the Alberta-British Columbia boundary, located at latitude 51 degrees, 43 minutes, longitude 116 degrees, 48 minutes, was named in his honour in 1920.
I think it is most unfortunate that so little is known about this expedition. For instance,
I find that Pierre Berton in his book, "The Mysterious North", on page 203 states that Captain Joseph Bernier, the bluff Canadian mariner and explorer, in a series of voyages during the early part of the century took possession of the Arctic for Canada. Evidently Mr. Berton, who is very well informed on Canadian history, particularly Arctic history, like the majority of other Canadians has never heard that Commander Low took possession of this area for Canada in 1904.
I made some other investigations. Apparently our university students, our high school students and our public school students have been completely misinformed to date on the history of Canadian exploration in the Arctic because of the failure to recognize this expedition and the lack of information concerning it.
I am going to make two or three suggestions before I sit down. I suggest that a copy of Commander Low's report-I understand there are two copies in existence here- his fragmentary diaries and any other papers that can be located be turned over to Dr. Kaye Lamb, our dominion archivist. I know that when it comes to ferreting out records concerning history Dr. Lamb has the eyes of a fox terrier, the nose of a retriever and the tenacity of a bulldog, and I think it would be most appropriate to give him the job of collecting this information and putting it in a safe place for future generations of Canadians.
My second suggestion is that advantage be taken of the fact that Dr. L. E. Borden, as the only known survivor of the expedition and, as I mentioned before, as the man who was the surgeon and botanist, has diaries, other notes, photographs, Eskimo art and recollections that would be invaluable in completing the records of the history of this first expedition into the Canadian Arctic. I hope the minister will find it convenient to arrange for the appropriate official of his department to visit Dr. Borden and take advantage of

the treasure of knowledge that he is able to supply the department and the archives.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I will certainly do that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
My third suggestion is that there is a splendid opportunity here for several organizations that have completely overlooked this expedition. To tell you the honest truth, I am amazed that the records of the Arctic institute were not more complete. I suggest that any one of the three following organizations have an opportunity to write a more or less popular edition of the history of our first Canadian expedition so that our university people, our high school children, the children in our public schools, Canadians generally and the members of the United States defence forces will have a proper knowledge of Canadian rights and sovereignty in the Arctic and when these regions were taken by Canada. I suggest that here is an opportunity for the Arctic Institute of Canada, the Canadian Geographical Society or the Canadian Historical Society. Any one of them is quite capable of using its magazine and other facilities to bring to the attention of the Canadian public this page in Canadian history which has been overlooked for many years. In my opinion every effort should be made through some such method as I have suggested to properly inform Canadians on this important question.
I also suggest that it would be a splendid gesture on the part of the Canadian board on geographical names to recognize the work done by Dr. L. E. Borden as surgeon and botanist, the first Canadian to botanize the Arctic, and for all his work in connection with this expedition, by naming some physical feature in Canada after him.
Finally I want to say that the Canadian Arctic belongs to Canada, and at this time it is most appropriate that we do not hesitate to emphasize our sovereign rights in that area and fully inform Canadians of the interesting history of that period.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
I want to say a few words on this occasion, though I do not intend to take too long. I noted what the minister said when he commenced his remarks about preferring to have the coal problem dealt with when the item comes up. However, it is very possible I will not be here on that occasion; therefore I should like to say something about the coal situation generally in Canada at this time.
I can assure him that if I should happen to be here then I will not repeat what I am about to say now.
First of all, I think the very distressing condition in which the coal industry finds
5, 1956	5695
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys itself hardly needs mention by me. I am not blaming anyone particularly for that because there are a number of factors entering into the problem. Probably the minister is not to blame in any particular instance but I think that the federal government, having in mind the over-all picture, could do a little more than is being done, and I will try to indicate what that is as I go along.
To emphasize the point I raised a moment ago about the alarming and distressing position in which the coal mining industry finds itself today, I should like to refer to the coal board report, page 10. This is the 1955 edition of the annual report, so it is right up to date. Under the heading "Developments in the Coal Situation and Current Outlook" it states:
The production of Canadian coal mines in 1954-55, amounting to 14*7 million tons, showed a decrease of 11 million tons from the total for 1953-54. This loss was borne by the Alberta and British Columbia fields and more than offset gains in those of Saskatchewan and the maritimes.
Then down further on the page we find this:
The full plight of the Canadian coal industry becomes manifest when it is considered that over the past four fiscal years the annual production has fallen by 3-8 million tons or 20-3 per cent, imports by 7-6 million tons or 29-4 per cent, and over-all consumption by 9-1 million tons or 21 1 per cent.
The decline in coal mining has occurred despite progressive and substantial increases in the financial assistance extended to it by the federal government. Subvention payments have risen from $4-6 million in 1951-52 to $11-3 million in 1954-55 and in the latter year exceeded those in 1953-54 by $1-5 million.
The Alberta and British Columbia fields, more especially the former, have suffered most of the aforenoted reduction in Canadian coal output. The present prospects for this segment of the industry are bleak. The bituminous mines, which used to supply about 70 per cent of their output to the railways, chiefly from their underground operations, have suffered further serious losses in this market.
I read that to you, Mr. Chairman, and to members of this committee in order to give the members of this house who represent all parts of Canada the facts regarding the distressing situation in which the coal industry finds itself. The situation is not peculiar to the western Canadian provinces. The same thing is true in the maritimes but to a lesser extent, and probably there is some reason for that. As I said a moment ago, Mr. Chairman, it is true that there is probably some reason for the decline in the coal industry, particularly in western Canada, where we have had the development of oil and gas. Oil has not taken too great a toll of the production of coal, but gas has taken some. But at the moment, particularly at
5696	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys the time at which this report was issued by the coal board, gas did not affect materially the production of coal; and by the statement I have read you can see that the production of coal has steadily declined.
To give you a more specific picture with regard to the decline of coal production let me further refer to the dominion coal board's report. At page 28, under the heading "Production", this is stated:
The output of Canadian coal mines during the fiscal year under review showed a reduction of $1,040,000 tons or 6-6 per cent in comparison with the total of 1953-54, and of 3,776,000 or 20-3 per cent as compared to the production of 1951-52. Most of this loss was borne by the Alberta fields.
That makes two occasions within a matter of a few pages in this report on which the board has pointed out that the coal industry in western Canada, and particularly in the province of Alberta, has been receiving very bad setbacks. As I say, that is not because of overuse in other parts of Canada of natural gas. It is true that the gas, when it comes down to Ontario, will affect to some extent the coal consumption in Ontario and in the province of Quebec. But there again it is not going to affect the production of coal in western Canada and in the maritimes as much as some would think, because very little coal from the other parts of Canada is used in those two central provinces anyway. We therefore cannot blame the situation on the use of fuel oil or gas, except of course to the extent that fuel oil particularly is being imported from the United States.
In this report we have the production figures for Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Saskatchewan, Alberta bituminous, Alberta subbituminous, British Columbia and Yukon. Let me give the total figure for 1953-54 which amounted to 15,803,000 tons. For 1954-55 it was 14,770,000 tons. That is the production for Canada. From the same report I want to give you the amount of coal which was imported into Canada from the United States; and may I say in passing that I think this is where our solution can be found. As to imports of bituminous coal, the total for 1954-55 was 15,639,000 tons. For anthracite the total was 2,504,000 tons. Those two figures make a total of 18,143,000 tons. You will notice there is a difference there of 3,373,000 tons of coal; that is, 3,373,000 more tons of coal were shipped into Canada than were produced in Canada.
When you consider that every year, according to the report, the production of coal has been dropping-since 1951-52 particularly- it seems to me that the federal government and the provinces also are going to be obliged to do something to see that this industry is


kept alive. I think every member in this house has on other occasions pointed out that the coal industry is vital to Canada from the standpoint of defence, if for no other reason. We are getting a gas line brought down to Ontario from which the Ontario people are going to derive a great advantage. But I must point out also that a gas line is most vulnerable from the standpoint of attack when the enemy come to invade this country, if they ever do.
We must be cautious that we do not destroy one of the greatest industries in Canada. In fact I do not think the time will ever come when you can completely do away with the coal mining industry and the need for coal. It might be reduced to some extent, but it certainly will never be done away with.
In his speech this afternoon the minister pointed out that a considerable amount of research has been done with regard to the coal-fired turbine. I think it is his hope and the hope of all of us that when that turbine is developed there might be some relief for our declining coal production. We have now spent

I think this is what the minister said; he will correct me if I am wrong

or by the end of the year will have spent something like $600,000-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
or $650,000 in the development of this new gas turbine engine. That is a tremendous amount of money, but that development has been going on for about four or five years. I can well recall that when the members of the house visited the plant at Montreal their hopes were raised that this machine was going to come into use in a year or two years at the most. We have been waiting now for many years longer than that, and there is no immediate prospect of that happening in the near future or of it being of assistance to the coal mining industry. We cannot, therefore, place too great hopes in that direction for immediate relief at least.
Then there are the experiments being conducted by the federal government in close co-operation with the provinces, particularly the province of Alberta, in connection with the development of electricity through the use of steam produced bycoal. That is probably going to assist coal production to some extent, particularly when the coal fields are in close proximity to the place where electricity is to be developed and when that electricity can be used for the development of industry. However, that, too, is a long way off, and we cannot put our immediate hopes in that direction if we wish to find a permanent solution for this declining coal industry.

I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that in this country we do not hesitate to go to great lengths to assist other lagging industry. My mind goes to the gold mining industry. There is never any objection in this house, or very little, particularly from the members from central Canada, when it comes to assisting the gold mining industry. I just want to put on the record something about the subsidies which have been paid to that industry. I am not overlooking the fact, either, that there have been subsidies paid to the coal industry as well, and I have already so indicated. It should be recalled that there are only about 23,000 people, I think it is, employed in the gold mining industry, and that is a very small number of people compared to the thousands and thousands who are employed in the coal industry. Our coal industry, however, is gradually going down and unemployment is resulting in Alberta from that fact. A year ago the provincial government allotted over $100,000 to reallocate and rehabilitate the miners who had been thrown out of employment because our coal industry was declining so rapidly.
But the gold industry is not declining quite so quickly. In 1948 we paid $10,546,000 in gold mining assistance; in 1949, $12,569,000; 1950,	$9,015,000;	1951,	$10,750,000;	1952,
$10,852,000; 1953, $14,625,000; 1954, $14 million; 1955, $10 million. It is estimated that in 1956 we will pay $11 million. This will make a total of $103,357,000 for that nine-year period. The coal industry, as I indicated, in 1951-52 received $4-6 million and in 1954-55, $11-3 million. When you compare the two you find that the gold mining industry, which employs a comparatively few people compared with the coal industry, has been assisted to a far greater extent than the coal industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend has been misinformed. I think the numbers employed in the two industries are approximately equal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I would ask the minister to put the exact figures on record, if he would, because my information is that there are only about 23,000 miners employed in the gold mining industry. That does not include their families, but I think there would be many times more than that employed in the coal industry. Of course I would agree with the minister that the number employed in the coal industry has been reduced tremendously in the last year because of reduced production and the closing of mines. As I indicated a moment ago, Alberta had to devote $100,000 to the rehabilitation of miners in that province and in order that they may move to other places. I would say that the
5, 1956	5697
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys number employed in the coal industry has reduced very rapidly from 1951 or 1948. It has been decreasing so rapidly we should be alarmed in this house lest the industry disappear entirely. Hon. members are aware of the fact that you just cannot train a miner overnight. If we were called upon to increase our coal production in case of emergency, we just could not do it because we would not have the qualified miners at hand to go back into those mines. We should, therefore, look very carefully at that aspect of it.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, as I have suggested before and as others have suggested, particularly the hon. member for Cape Breton South, that we should have a national fuel policy. You will recall that the federal government, particularly the Prime Minister, was not hesitant about declaring that we should have a national gas policy for Canada when there was some thought that gas from Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba might be shipped south to the United States and deprive Ontario and Quebec of that cheap fuel for the development of the industries ir those two central provinces. The government then came out most hastily and said no, sir; we shall have a national gas policy in Canada and an all-Canadian pipe line.
Why can we not show some of that same concern and anxiety for the coal industry and establish a national fuel policy for Canada? As indicated a few moments ago, we are importing from the United States 3,373,000 tons of coal more than we produce in all Canada. I think that is where our solution lies. Some may say that I am trying to cut off imports from the United States, and if you are going to do it in one thing you should do it in another. Make no mistake about it; the manufacturing industries which are established in the central provinces do that very thing. They have great protection from the tariffs of this country which allow only limited amounts of the goods they are manufacturing to come in from the United States.
I think it would not be unfair at all for the Canadian government to say, we shall reduce the imports of coal from the United States at least to the point where there is some semblance of equality between the amount shipped in from the United States and the amount we produce in this country. I am going to say, as I said last year, that if we would only reduce imports from the United States by one million tons, which would not affect imports from the United States to any great extent, we would be able to give this dying Canadian coal industry a greatly needed shot in the arm. If we were to curtail imports from the United States by two million

Supply

Mines and Technical Surveys tons it would do a lot toward re-establishing our industry, regardless of the fact that gas is going to be used in Ontario and Quebec. If we would curtail the importation of coal from the United States to the extent of four million tons, I am sure that our industry would be put back on its feet again.
Then what would be the over-all situation? I do not think it would be unfair at all. I do not think anyone could accuse me of being against the United States coal or fuel oil industry in endeavouring to get a market in Canada for some of our own production. I say, what would be the over-all picture then? Instead of a production of 14,770,000 tons in Canada we would have 18,770,000 tons. Instead of 18,183,000 tons coming in from the United States we would have 14,143,000 tons.
I am going to say that while we would be producing in Canada about 3} million or 4 million tons more than we would be importing, it would be a healthy condition for this country. We should not be importing more coal from the United States than we produce in Canada when we have practically 7 per cent of the world's known supply of coal in this country, and particularly when our own coal mines are being closed down and our miners thrown out of work all across the country. That is true of the maritimes and western Canada as well. If that were done it would give our mines a needed shot in the arm, if I may use that expression.
I say to the minister I recognize immediately that the government has given the coal industry quite a lot of money in the way of subventions, but not nearly as much as the gold mining industry has been receiving. I do not believe the minister would be able to raise subventions sufficiently high to offset the tremendous amount of coal that is coming in from the United States. I think a limit has to be put on the importation of coal into this country. If that were done the subvention on coal would not have to be raised too much.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: How would you do it; how would you limit it?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It would be very easy to put a limit on the maximum amount of coal that could be shipped into this country. I do not see any difficulty at all. The United States puts a limit on the amount of agricultural products that can be shipped from Canada into the United States. Why can we not put a limit on the amount of coal shipped into Canada from the United States?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: To what extent will the steel mills in Canada accept coal from Alberta, from the point of view of quantity?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
There is a remark on that in the coal board's report, if I could just lay my hands on it. They speak about that. On page 11 I find the following:
The main hope for new outlets for western coal lies in the field of increased thermal power generation.
No, that is not it. They mention it, but I just cannot lay my hands on it. They mention the fact that one of the hopes for an increased production of western coal lies in the amount supplied to industrial plants in Ontario. I think the importation of gas into Ontario and Quebec from Alberta will have some effect on that. I say to the minister that although we are giving a generous amount in subventions, I do not think that is going to be the solution of our coal problem. It does seem to me that we have to do something about the importation of this coal into Canada, at least to the amount necessary to keep our mines going and to give our employees a decent standard of living. If we did that it would be the solution of our coal problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

I have had the figures of the number of employees in the gold mining industry supplied to me. In 1954, 18,479 people were employed in the gold mining industry and in 1953, the year for which the figures are supplied here, 18,291 were employed in the coal industry.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take any more of the time of this committee than is necessary, but I hope I will be permitted to make a few comments concerning the activities of the department and its personnel. There are also one or two things which I would like to bring to the attention of the minister, the officers of his department and hon. members who, I am sure, are all interested in this very important sector of the government.
At the outset I wish to congratulate the minister on the high efficiency with which he directs the affairs of his ministry. I also

wish to congratulate each and every one in the department on the excellent work done during the past year. More particularly I want to pay a tribute to the engineers, the surveyors, the geologists and other experts of the department and their helpers whose work in the field or at headquarters has proven to be so valuable to the orderly development of our mineral and other natural resources.
They have been working in co-operation with other provincial or private scientific research parties and with the prospectors and mine developers, and with them they share much of the credit for this extraordinary development which has taken place in northern Canada during the last 15 or 20 years. Without the work of all, this tremendous sweep of waste land to the north could not have become productive regions dotted with wealth-producing communities.
I am also pleased to see that the minister has again authorized the publication of a pamphlet summarizing the activities of his department for the year 1955. Everyone who is acquainted with this pamphlet agrees that it is an excellent publication and that it should be continued.
I wish to put on record short extracts from some of the letters I have received commenting on this booklet. The committee will be pleased to hear what the industry thinks of this department. The first letter is from F. J. O'Connell, general manager of Sigma Mines (Quebec) Limited. I quote:
We were very pleased to receive Summary of Activities, 1954 for the department of mines. We have reviewed this thoroughly, find it most informative and are amazed at the number of activities carried on under the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
The next letter is from the manager of Elder Mines Limited, and reads as follows:
I particularly liked the Summary of Activities of 1954, published by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I think they did a very thorough job and are to be congratulated in turning out this publication.
Another letter comes from the manager of Stadacona Mines Limited, and reads as follows:
The Summary of Activities, 1954, acquaints the reader with the scope of the department of mines and the various services performed. It is gratifying to note that the geological survey is expanding so rapidly and that they are employing more aircraft in their operations.
The last one I wish to put on record is from the manager of the Lamaque Mining Company Limited, and it reads as follows:
The Summary of Activities of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys for 1954 is a very well prepared booklet and it was interesting to note the modern methods which this department is now using not only to increase the speed
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys at which geological studied areas are being mapped but it also shows the very desirable trend in increasing efficiency of the work of this department. We note that the "New Quebec-Labrador, Quebec" areas were covered by a total of ten field parties and that only the province of British Columbia exceeded this number of field parties. This suggests that the department realize the importance of the possible mineral deposits in our province.
This booklet, Mr. Chairman, is published in English and in French. It is well presented, and it certainly makes it easier for whoever wishes to acquaint himself with the activities of the department or intends to discuss its estimates. What I like most about this pamphlet is that it gives concise information on the main accomplishments in every one of the five branches into which the department is divided.
For instance, if we look at the map on page 2 we are immediately aware of the number and diversity of the locations across the country which were visited by hydrographic, topographical and geodetic field survey parties during the course of last season's operations. Also on pages 22 and 23, at a glance we are informed of the different locations visited by the field parties of the geological survey branch during the summer of 1955. The whole pamphlet is very informative, and again I express the hope that its publication will be continued.
Despite the long association of mining with Canada, it was only about 55 years ago that it actually became a large industry in this country. During those 55 years, the number and importance of the mines have increased to the point where, for 1955, the value of their output has been more than $1,500 million. Canada has become one of the world's greatest producers of minerals. There is every reason to believe that in this country of ours during the next ten years we shall see an even greater expansion in our mining industry than we enjoyed during the past decade, and we know that was the most active decade we ever had.
There are two more items concerning which I would like to say a few words before closing these remarks. The first item has to do with radioactivity surveys; the other has to do with gold. Concerning the radioactivity surveys I wish to learn from the minister if we have made any progress. In the summary of activities for 1950 and 1951 we were informed as follows, and I quote from page 21 of the 1950 report:
In co-operation with the national research council and with the crown-owned Eldorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited, work was commenced on the development of an airborne radioactive detector that may be used to locate deposits of radioactive substances from an aircraft. It may thus soon be possible to make both

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys magnetic and radioactivity surveys at the same time. Considerable further research work is needed, however, before any claims for effective application are justified.
The following year, as reported at page 22 of the 1951 report, it was stated:
An airborne detector of radioactivity was carried in the same plane as the magnetometer, and radioactivity surveys were made at the same time as the magnetic. So far, however, this instrument has not been shown to be useful as a geological tool. When the anomalies noted are better understood the instrument may prove to be valuable for prospecting for uranium deposits.
Can the minister tell the committee if the geophysics section of his department has made any progress as far as this method of survey is concerned? Can we expect that the geological survey branch will be able to issue maps containing this kind of information?
The last item with which I wish to deal is gold. The mines branch of the department is continually engaged in activities concerned with all phases of the mining and metal industries. In every one of the annual reports we read that the different divisions of this branch are carrying on research work of all kinds. In the case of the industrial minerals the branch is always directing much of its efforts to research relating to the development, utilization and conservation of our mineral resources. In a pamphlet published during the month of March 1956 by the Canadian metal mining association I note the following:
Research Into Extended Commercial Uses of Gold.
Following a resolution sent to this association by the Quebec metal mining association, the executive committee of the board have under consideration a proposal that the possibility of research into more extensive commercial uses of gold be examined.
This question has been raised previously, and for the guidance of our board we are anxious to obtain as much information as possible concerning previous investigations and their results.

Although the minister has made a comprehensive statement, there are one or two suggestions and questions I should like to address to him. We have had a reasonably full discussion of the problems of the gold mining industry and they have been disposed of for this session, and I shall not say any more on that score. There are one or two aspects of mining taxation to which


I think the minister might give some thought with a view to a conference with the Minister of Finance in the general interests of the best use of taxation to encourage mining.
The immense growth in the value of Canada's metal mine production, from $42 million in 1907 to $763 million in 1954, has not come about simply because there was ore available. We have had provisions in our fiscal arrangements for realistic depletion allowances, nontaxation of capital gains-though that seems to have got into an area of uncertainty- freedom from income tax for the first three years of a new mine's production, and important permissible deductions from taxable income of expenditure made for mining exploration and development.
There are aspects of these last two which I should like to mention. The three-year tax-free period to permit a mine to recover some of the capital costs of constructing its mill and installing its mining plant, under the present legislation, is a continuous period.
I am not sure whether such instances have arisen, but one has come to my attention which might well arise, where through no fault of the management of the mine the three-year period has begun to run and production has been interrupted. It might be interrupted for a number of causes beyond the control of the operators-acts of God and the King's enemies, as they are usually described-such as unusual storms or prolonged strikes. A variety of things could interrupt the intended benefits of the three-year period for a very considerable time, to the detriment of the mine, and the mine would lose the opportunity to recover the capital costs which this tax-free period was intended to permit it to recover.
I suggest to the minister that he consider with the Minister of Finance the desirability of giving the Department of National Revenue authority to permit the suspension of the running of the period in those cases so the benefit is not lost. That is not an important or far-reaching matter, but it seems to me that it would be a desirable precaution against that contingency. In the Income Tax Act, which this house has under consideration, there is a provision, and I shall use the words, if I may, of the Ontario mining association in describing this problem-
Section 21, subsection 4 of the bill . . .
That is Bill No. 418.
. . . sets up a new subsection (8a) which provides that where an oil or mining corporation acquires the property of an oil corporation, it may deduct the undistributed exploration expense incurred by the predecessor corporation. This simply permits the said oil or mining corporation to adopt the same practice with respect to deferred items of

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
this kind in the predecessor company as it follows with respect to its own current development expenses.
The anomaly existing is that while the mining company is empowered to do this with respect to a predecessor oil company which it may acquire, it is not authorized to take similar action in the event that it acquires a predecessor mining company.

I know it has been customary for the minister to keep his discussion of the coal industry until we have reached that item, but now that he has permitted some discussion on this item I think it is only logical that we should follow through with it. I understand that the chairman of the coal board is away attending a conference at the present time, and it is rather uncertain when he will get back. As far as I am concerned, I am particularly interested in the problem of coal, and under the present circumstances I think it requires discussion at this time.
I too should like to say that since the present minister has taken over the department there has been more order and sanity in its administration. I remember when it was just an orphan, and any discussions we had in the house were rather uncertain and very ambiguous. The minister has done a good job in preparing his reports. At least it is quite clear what the department is doing section by section, and while it is not going ahead as fast in some respects as we would like, nevertheless it is moving forward and not backward.
I listened to the hon. member for Bow River. The subject of coal is not a new one to him or me, because we have been discussing it for a long time in the house. I think his observations with respect to the importation of United States coal are timely, and that is perhaps the crux of our whole problem. But I should like to point out that there should not be any difficulty as far as the government is concerned in carrying out what he suggested, namely the placing of an embargo on a certain amount of United States coal coming into this country and zoning markets so there would be markets for coal produced in Canada. Such action should be taken because of the very heavy imports from the United States.
The largest single import into this country measured in terms of dollars is coal. It is the largest single item in our whole import list. As the hon. member for Bow River said, we import 4,700,000 tons more than we produce. Why I say it should not be difficult for the government to arrange what he suggested is that more than half of that 4,700,000


tons is imported by the Canadian National Railways, a government-owned organization. It should not be difficult to come to some understanding with Canadian National Railways on the marketing of Canadian coal at least between Ontario and the maritimes.
I have taken the matter up a good many times with the president of the C.N.R. in the committee on railways and shipping, and of course his answer always is that Canadian coal must be made competitive. They accept no social responsibility at all for communities across the country, and neither do the companies that mine the coal. They accept no social responsibility for the communities where they are exploiting the raw material. Until such time as governments take action to bring to their attention the fact that they have some social responsibility to the communities they are exploiting, the situation will go on as it is, as long as it is measured in terms of dollars and cents and figures on the right side of the ledger.
May I say here that I do not hold the federal government entirely responsible, because they have very little control over the coal mining industry of this country. In the first place, the provincial governments grant the leases. They are the custodians of the raw materials of the provinces, and they hold them in trust for the people of the provinces. When they farm them out to large companies and give them leases in perpetuity the first responsibility rests with the provincial governments and the companies that hold the leases. The federal government's only prerogative is the granting of subventions, subsidies and drawbacks, and the coal board will also assist in marketing in so far as they have the power to do so. Under the British North America Act the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the dominion coal board are going as far as they are permitted to go, unless the provinces change their minds and there is a change of heart on the part of the operating companies. Until we get legislation placing some power in the hands of the federal government the thing will go along as it is.
The hon. member for Bow River also spoke about the coal-burning gas turbine engine being experimented with at McGill. He stated that the members who went down to see the project some four or five years ago were very enthusiastic about it. I want to remind him that I was one of the members who visited the project at that time and, as the minister knows, I was not enthusiastic about it. It was being held up at that time as the great solution so far as the future of the coal mining industry was concerned,

and the newspapers were full of it. But after I visited there my conclusion was that if it ever worked it was at least ten years away from any commercial value. That is five years ago and it is still in the experimental stage.
The assumption is that the turbine engine is interchangeable with the present diesel engines recently adopted by the Canadian National Railways. That is not true, because in order to instal the turbine engine in a locomotive a special locomotive will have to be built for it, and having in mind the huge investment in diesels made by the C.N.R. in the last few years they are not going to write off that investment in the foreseeable future.
I think it is well to dispel these illusions that are thrown out from time to time to keep people guessing and wondering for a year or two while at the same time there is a rapid decline in the industry. I do not think it does any good, and I think the department is fully aware of that fact.
In that regard I should like to refer to page 90 of the 1955 departmental report. What they say is not very encouraging, "but at the same time they are not trying to fool anybody. The report has this to say:
This equipment, which is installed at the gas dynamics laboratory of McGill University at Ste. Anne de Bellevue, was operated for about 300 hours during the year. Some difficulties were experienced with slag formation and corrosion of the tubes in the hot heat exchangers. The causes of these troubles and methods for their prevention are being investigated.
That is just about where it was five years ago. The phrase used there indicating that it was operated for about 300 hours might give the impression that it was installed as an engine and had operated for that number of hours. Actually it is just sitting there on a frame and the engine has been operated. The difficulty is and has been to find a cooling system that will take away the heat from the gas and not burn off the blades of the engine. That has been the difficulty and I think it still is the difficulty. If the engine is ever perfected I think it might be a good marine engine or a good engine for the generation of thermal power in small electric plants, but I cannot see Canadian National Railways writing off their huge investment in diesels within the foreseeable future and building new locomotives to instal that type of engine.
The reason I am saying this is that for too long there has been too much of this kind of thing thrown out to people, and it is merely an illusion and raises false hopes. I believe we should be frank and realistic at this time with the people in an industry such as the

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys coal mining industry. As the minister knows, at this time one has to be careful in discussing coal, particularly in my end of the country. As the minister also knows, the mine workers have been conducting negotiations with the operating company for several months. They had a conciliation board, and the conciliation board decided that no wage increases or changes in conditions were warranted at this time because of the financial position of the coal company. A vote was taken on that proposal and the miners rejected it by about three to one. Now they are going to hold a convention for the purpose of determining where they go from there.
I do not want to get involved in any of the internal problems, but I would say this. The miners have worked hard and have co-operated fully. They have subsidized to a large extent that coal operation in Nova Scotia. They have not had any adjustment in wages or conditions since 1952. At the same time alongside of them, within 13 miles, is the steel plant owned by the same corporation they work for; and in that steel plant there has been a continuous adjustment upward in wages, working conditions, fringe benefits and additional holidays. To those 7,000 or 8,000 men who always led in the wage field in that province it is a rather tough proposition to see every other industry stepping up ahead of them while they continue to accept the same conditions and wages that prevailed back in 1952.
What the outcome of their negotiations is-going to be one cannot say at this time. But there is something the minister's department can do in co-operation with the Department of Transport. It is rather difficult to pinpoint any particular problem, especially an economic one, as that of any one department because they spill over from one into the other. The recent 7 per cent interim increase in freight rates which has just been authorized by the board of transport commissioners has added a problem to those of the department of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, in that it adds 12 cents a ton to the cost of the movement of coal from Nova Scotia to the points at which it is marketed. Some is marketed in Ontario but it is mostly marketed in Quebec. That increase of 12 cents a ton together with the other 7 per cent or 7J- per cent increase when it goes into operation some time this fall will bring the increase up to about 24 cents a ton. That adds to the burden.
In the past, when an increase in freight rates was made, it was the practice of the coal board to revise the subvention schedule so as to absorb the additional freight-rate cost and maintain the same balance in the freight
5704	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys rates for the movement of coal. A few days ago I asked the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys whether it was the intention to follow the practice of the past and absorb into the subvention this 12 cents a ton additional freight rate for the movement of Nova Scotia coal. The minister's answer at that time was, of course, that no consideration had been given to that matter at that time. Before we conclude consideration of his estimates I hope the minister will tell us whether the matter has been further considered, and whether the practice of the past is to be carried out.
As I said a moment ago, if one follows the press on this question of the future of coal and the economic feasibility of natural gas and other fuels, one is left in a rather confused state of mind. When you pick up one press clipping you find that it says, "Golden year for coal is seen". This is from the United States, where they are stepping up production and they figure there is a bright future for coal. Then you pick up an editorial and read, "Coal comes back", and so on. That sounds rather nice except to the coal miners, who cannot see it coming back as far *as their wages and conditions are concerned.
Then recently the president of the coal company in his annual report to the board of directors-they held the meeting in Nova Scotia this time, for the first time in the history of the corporation-stated as follows:
. . . the impact upon the coal mining industry in Nova Scotia of the St. Lawrence seaway and the trans-Canada pipe line is "somewhat difficult to appraise and foresee". He added, however, that "neither one of these projects appeared to offer other than somewhat alarming possibilities of increased competition in our upper Canadian markets".
And so on. Then he offers as a solution mechanization, lower costs and greater production. I have heard that story a good many times during my lifetime; sweat it out of the hides of the workers; take it from the consumer; we take no responsibility except you get down and dig. In another editorial-and this is from the old country-they finish up by saying this:
Thus oil which now accounts for about 38 per cent of the free world's energy supplies, will soon displace coal from the dominant position it has hitherto held.
We have one press statement against the other. One expert says coal is on the way out. The other fellow says there is a golden future for it. The president of the big operating coal company says sweat it out of their hides and get the figures on the right side of the balance sheet. As I said before, until we get a realization of responsibility on the part of those who are fortunate in having huge leases granted by provincial governments
IMr. GiUis.l

that prevent anyone else from operating-and provincial governments grant charters to enable them to amalgamate five or six companies in one; squeeze the small shareholders out; establish remote control at Mount Royal; draw big salaries and pay taxes in Quebec; siphon the wealth off from that part of the country-until we bring these people to the realization that they have some social responsibility in the communities where they work on the natural resources, we are going to continue this thing of ghost towns everywhere we are working in a wasting industry such as mining; whether it is coal, gold or metal of any kind, it is a wasting resource.
I was encouraged by this press report recently from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald.
I think it is the first realistic step that has been taken for a long time. It is headed "To make special study of coal industry in N.S." and it reads in part as follows:
The Gordon royal commission on Canada's economic prospects will make a "special study'' of the Nova Scotia coal industry, the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, was informed Tuesday by a top official of district 26, united mine workers of America.
A union statement said the Gordon commission has ordered that "a special study be conducted into all aspects of the Nova Scotia coal industry".
The Montreal firm of Urwick, Currie Ltd. "has been engaged by the commission to further investigate the industry and report to the Gordon commission".
This is encouraging. The only thing I have to say on that point is this, Mr. Chairman. If that examination is made, I hope the people who make it are competent, are free from pressure and will call the shots across the board as they see them. I hope they will not do as previous commissions have done. I hope they will not just compile a rehash of briefs that I read 30 years ago and call it a report and an examination of that industry at this time.
Mr. Forsyth indicated he was fearful of what the St. Lawrence seaway and natural gas were going to do to the coal industry, when and if that pipe line reaches Quebec city. Six years ago I was a member of the committee that made the first examination of the application of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to build that famous line. At that time all those who appeared before the committee were from the United States, the engineers and the people who made the surveys. The Lehman banking people from New York were going to finance it, and they appeared before that committee.
I asked these witnesses what they calculated natural gas in Montreal and Quebec would do to the coal industry of Nova Scotia, which was the main economic base of that province. Well, they said they did not know.

I said, was any survey made east of Montreal? No, no survey was made. Were there any representations from the operating coal companies? There were no representations from anyone. This was just the forgotten area. They wrote Canada off at Quebec city.
As the minister knows, they were good enough to hear the only witness we could get with any information on the subject, the chairman of the dominion coal board. He came and gave evidence. He admitted that gas and oil had pretty well cleaned up the coal industry of Alberta, but that province was fortunate in that these other industries replaced the coal industry. We do not have that. What is going to happen when gas reaches Quebec and Montreal? We do not know. It is a hypothetical question.
This was six years ago and the line has not been completed yet, so we have had a lease on life. I talked with one of these witnesses afterwards, and I asked him by how much they could undersell coal. He said they could take the market from coal in any industry except the basic steel industry. He said they could take it from coal in the domestic field, that they could undersell coal by at least $1.50 per ton, measuring it in B.T.U.'s. He said, "If we did not figure we would get that market in Montreal and Quebec we would not be going down there." That is logical; they require that market.
I have always questioned in my mind the economic wisdom of taking gas from Alberta to Quebec and Montreal. I do not think that is going to be cheap fuel for that area. I do not think it is a good development, because you have approximately half of Canada's total productive capacity concentrated in that area and you are harnessing industry and domestic heating to a long pipe line going straight across the country, which would be extremely vulnerable. If you changed over your equipment it would take a long time to change back if something happened to that pipe line. Then there is the question of supply. While geologists and oil men may make guesses as to how long the oil is going to last, I think you can be more certain about solid fuels. I am not so sure you can be certain about either oil or gas.
I have a brief in my hand prepared by the solid fuels research institute. These people should know something about the subject. Of course, they have a motive in trying to retain solid fuels, but at the same time it is a rather responsible body. On page 1 of the brief they say:
A study of newspaper clippings on many American centres will show a record of frequent failure of supply, of low pressures, forced cut-offs
5, 1956	5705
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys and rising prices. For many communities depending on natural gas, these have been disturbing factors.
This brief points up this question in quite a realistic way. They go on and say, on page 2:
A stable coal industry is recognized as a necessity. The economic flow of solid fuel for Ontario and western Quebec region is from an area within a radius of 500 miles.
They are talking about United States coal.
Many questions have been raised as to the economic soundness of a 2,000 mile pipe line.
That has always stuck in my mind, too. I would question the wisdom, in a time of rumours of war, threats of war and the possibility of the hydrogen bomb, of harnessing the industrial section of Quebec to a pipe line that is over 2,000 miles long and is certainly vulnerable to sabotage. As I said before, if you change your heating facilities and something happens to that line, then you are in quite a spot.
Personally I do not think the operating coal companies in Nova Scotia particularly, are pulling their share of the load. Right in my own area they closed down three fairly large mines since the mechanization program went into effect. So far the results of the mechanization program have confirmed all the doubts I had as to its value in stepping up production and cheapening costs in these old submarine mines. It has not been very successful to date, and it has had a fairly good test period. Whether or not the companies are trying to find markets for coal or whether they are producing coal to fill the markets, I am rather doubtful. Just a few days ago I received a telegram from Toronto which reads:
We may need 50 tons per day of pulverized coal for a project at Bancroft, Ontario. Would like to use Cape Breton coal. Where do I inquire for established prices f.o.b. destination. Please wire or phone collect.
I telephoned this man and he told me that the 50 tons would perhaps be stepped up, and it would be a continuing order. Well, 50 tons a day is a fairly substantial order, but he could not find anyone in the province of Ontario through whom he could place an order or get quotations. They are certainly not trying to sell coal in Ontario. This man told me that the reason he wanted coal was that he had been using oil and had found it expensive. He wanted to get out of it.
When you talk about coal being competitive with oil, that is a pretty good example. Here is a man who is using oil, and he wants to get out of it and go back to pulverized coal. If these people are trying to sell coal why is there not an agent in that area? At least if you are trying to sell neckties or shoes or aluminum ware, there is an agent going
5706	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys around offering it to you. There is a possibility that there is that kind of business running around Ontario if they wished to go after it.
Perhaps these companies are too busy marketing United States coal. Dominion Coal has a wholly-owned subsidiary in Montreal, the Dominion Import Company, and perhaps they are too busy doing that. That is something I hope the Gordon commission will go into quite thoroughly.
I think the federal government in so far as they can under the circumstances, have done a reasonable job in assisting the industry by way of subventions, subsidies, drawbacks and rebates under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. If you look at the assistance these people have received and then look at their balance sheets you will find they would not be in business at all if it were not for the help they get from the federal government. But they take this position. We want your help but we are free enterprisers; you have nothing to say about where we spend your money or how we invest it or whether we market the coal or whether we do not market the coal; that is our business and it is none of your business. According to the figures I have of the assistance they get from the balance sheets they put out, if public support were withdrawn from them they would be insolvent.
I have a quarrel with them on another score. At a convention in Toronto the Prime Minister said that when the maritimes took the initiative and began to make plans to do things for themselves the federal government would help. Well, since that time they have been doing something. The Atlantic economic council is doing an excellent job probing the possibilities of intermarketing among the four maritime provinces, what they can produce here and what they can market there. Some little industries have been established; not big ones, but it is something. They are doing something.
The four premiers of the Atlantic provinces are meeting in Fredericton to ascertain what can be done further. Well, what is the answer? What can be done to bolster a waning coal industry? The answer is subsidiary industries. A few days ago the president of Dosco made the statement that they were establishing two new fabricating plants this year. I was very sorry to learn they were not going to be established in Nova Scotia; they were going to be established in Quebec. That man was a member of the Atlantic economic council. That is the kind of industry that is required in the maritimes to bolster the economy if coal is in the shaky position that is indicated at
IMr. Gillis.]

this time, and if those people are interested in those communities where they are working on the raw materials, because those fabricating plants in Quebec are going to be supplied with the raw material from Sydney, from the basic steel plant where they have the iron ore, the coal, the limestone and all the ingredients that will go into the steel that will be fabricated there. It will all come from that area. Why could not at least one of those plants be established there if those people had any social responsibility, because that is the base of their whole empire? The raw materials will be taken from that area.
Of course when they turn out that raw steel they will get a subvention-

Those two paragraphs from the minister's letter tell a great deal and are worth pondering. I believe it would pay the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to work in cooperation with the Minister of Labour in reviewing the situation. If they wished they could set up a committee; it could even be a parliamentary committee, which might be a good idea. It also might be an interdepartmental committee, with members of a miners' union and members of the coal mining industry, if they wish. Some body should be set up to investigate whether or not it is possible to rehabilitate the coal mining industry, with special emphasis on the rehabilitation of the coal miner who is in a very bad way because after all, as the hon. member for Bow River said, you cannot train a coal miner overnight. You cannot go out on the street and say to an individual, "I will give you a job digging coal". These are specially trained men; mining is a life work. These men go in the mines when they are young and they stay there and put their whole life into their work. If at middle age or later they find themselves unemployed by reason of depressed conditions in the coal mines they are in need of rehabilitation, because they are on in years and there is little else they can do. It is very bad for them.
In this report of the Alberta government's committee on rehabilitation it states that in one year alone the total placements were 384 families who were moved with their effects. In another year 325 families were moved into other areas, where they were rehabilitated and found other employment. I shall read one paragraph of the report:
In carrying out its work, the miners' rehabilitation committee wishes to express its appreciation for the valuable assistance rendered by the national employment service and the united mine workers of America, district 18.
Well, $100,000 was appropriated for this purpose. It was found that it was not necessary to spend all the money, because they received such excellent co-operation from these bodies. I shall not say anything more. This must be about the twentieth or twenty-first annual speech I have made on coal. Perhaps they have not been very effective; otherwise something would have been done by this time. But this is the twenty-first year I have been sitting here, and I do not think I have let a year go by without dinning into the ears of the government the need for a national coal policy and trying to do what I can for the coal mining industry of my own constituency and of Canada generally.

It seems that in this particular session the situation is graver than it ever was before. I can only suggest this to the minister. We live in an age of progress. We are building a pipe line that is going to take the place of a great deal of coal in eastern Canada, in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. As I said on a previous occasion, who knows but that it will not be very many years until atomic energy will displace that again? That is the way it goes. Millions and millions of tons of coal are lying in the ground. Perhaps it will continue to lie in the ground until this earth is destroyed and eventually becomes recreated in so many millions of years, with a new race of people who will have to start all over again and commence digging coal. Perhaps that will be the situation.
I shall not say any more, but I wish the minister would tell the coal mining industry exactly what the score is and then take steps to remedy that situation.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks this evening will differ from those of previous speakers. I was most interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West this afternoon, when he dealt with the forgotten expedition into the Arctic in 1903 and 1904 by Commander A. P. Low. It appears strange to me, as I am sure it does to all members of the house, that proper notice was not taken of this historic expedition for many years, in spite of the loss of the proclamation records. I am glad to report,

however, that the Arctic exploration publication of December, 1955 properly deals with this expedition. It is to be hoped that the Canadian Geographical Journal will take the opportunity to publish an article correctly describing this famous expedition, the first Canadian expedition into the Arctic.
This afternoon I followed with interest the remarks of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys dealing with the activities of his department. The minister and his officials have always been eager and willing to cooperate in all matters pertaining to the mining industry in general. They are to be congratulated on the efficiency of their department and for doing an excellent job.
While I am on my feet I wish to take this occasion to say something about the Canadian Geographical Society and the monthly magazine published under its auspices, namely the Canadian Geographical Journal. The Canadian Geographical Society is one of the most public spirited and unselfish organizations in this country. Its ambition is to make Canada better known to Canadians and to the rest of the world. Its chief purpose is to distribute information on the geography, resources and people of this country. To assist in this task, and as its primary object, the society publishes the magazine to which I have referred. The Canadian Geographical Journal in my view is one of the very best periodicals issued anywhere in Canada. In a sense it is the eyes of this nation, because through its illustrated and printed pages it enables Canadians and other people to see this country as an entity.
The Journal writers take threads or fragments of Canada's history and geography and over the years weave or blend these into a meaningful and informative picture of Canada as a whole, in all its interest and variety. In a word, it serves to present a memorable image of Canada.
The Canadian Geographical Society was founded 27 years ago, in 1929, I believe, to be exact. Its first president was that great friend and native son of the Canadian north, Dr. Charles Camsell, C.M.G. Today its president is another great worker in advancing the best interests of northern Canada and other parts as well. Major General H. A. Young, who is also deputy minister of public works, is president of the society at the present time.

That is fine. Through good times and bad the society has managed to keep the Journal alive and issued regularly. How they do this on the funds available to the society thus far, baffles me. In the 67509-3634
5, 1956	5711
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys United States the corresponding publication has the benefit of very large sums bequeathed by wealthy, public spirited citizens. In Canada there is nothing resembling this type of large-scale financial assistance for a geographical publication. Nevertheless the articles in the Canadian Geographical Journal are of a high calibre and its pages are always handsomely illustrated, sometimes in several colours. Colour printing is a particularly expensive process, however, and I imagine it is a special luxury at present for the Journal.
The success thus far of this Canadian magazine is due in large measure, I believe, to a dedicated board of directors, a wise editorial committee and a very able executive secretary and editor of publications in the person of Gordon M. Dallyn. Incidentally, all directors and committee members serve without remuneration.
The society does much more than publish its worthy journal. It sponsors public lectures and awards scholarships as well as granting financial aid to exploration projects and other research. Its sponsored lectures have been given by such men as Sir Hubert Wilkins, General McNaughton, Dr. MacKintosh Bell, Edward Shackleton and Gordon Robertson, deputy minister of northern affairs and national resources. In addition the society awards scholarships in geography. In the years 1939 to 1953, 29 such scholarships were awarded amounting to a total of $7,400.
In the matter of expenditures to assist exploration, financial aid was contributed by the society to the Baffin islands expedition of 1950 and 1953; to Dr. Williams for geographical investigation in the Churchill region; to Dr. Kimble and associates for a survey of the St. Maurice valley; and to a Mr. Laforest with the upper Orinoco expedition. In addition to sponsoring the production of several documentary films with geographical themes, the society has published and distributed over 5 million pamphlets containing articles from its Journal on 153 separate subjects. It is an astonishing fact that when the Canadian Geographical Society first came into existence there was not one professional geographer in Canada. Today there are over 300.
This year for the first time on record the association of American geographers met outside the United States. Montreal was the city chosen in this connection, and this gesture in itself is a tribute to Canada's significance in the world geographical picture. The international geographical union, which meets every four years, convenes in August this year in Rio de Janeiro. Canada has always been a member of this world organization. For many years the Canadian
5712	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and. Technical Surveys Geographical Society was the nominal sponsor of the Canadian committee of the international geographical union. I am glad to say that Canada will be represented at the Rio meeting this year by Dr. Norman Nicholson, head of the geographical branch, Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I believe that every consideration and support ought to be given by the federal government and by Canadian citizens individually and generally to this organization created to foster greater geographical knowledge.
What are some of the ways in which geographical science helps Canada and Canadians? First, it assists us all to understand better the economic development now taking place in this country. A better knowledge of geography, of the distribution of our natural resources, of fuel supplies and needs -all of these facts help Canadians to grasp in a more intelligent way just what is involved in the concept, engineering and economics of the various projects being undertaken throughout the length and breadth of Canada today. I mention as an example the gas pipe line from Alberta to eastern Canada.
Second, geographical knowledge also enables Canadians generally to understand that in order properly to develop the mineral wealth of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, railways must be built. On this subject I want to point out that had it not been for Charles Camsell and his lifelong interest in the north, as well as his awareness and knowledge of the importance of the north country, our national development would have been much less extensive.
Third, by studies of the distribution of ice in northern waters, the action of currents and the influence of winds, our scientists are able to assist materially in solving the problems of ocean navigation along our northern coast.
Fourth, survey work in the north, carried out by parties operating under the direction of the geographical branch of the federal mines and technical surveys department, engaged in studying and recording surface conditions in the territories such as the location of navigable rivers, the extent and type of vegetation, the location of muskeg areas and so forth, has been of immeasurable aid in the construction of the D.E.W. line.
From these and many other activities we see that modern geography is not only a relatively new-found art but a vitally important practical science. It teaches us where our various resources are located. We learn about weather, climate and problems of transportation. We gain a better understanding of our own and other lands. It helps


us to dispel the curse of overspecialization in these days in a country where many graduates of our universities are actually ignorant of the character and resources of Canada, and have little appreciation of how their particular field of training relates to the well-being and progress of the country as a whole.
For all these reasons I would therefore strongly urge that the Canadian Geographical Society and its Canadian Geographical Journal are worthy of substantial federal government support in the form of an annual grant or vote. I urge this for a reason even greater than any I have thus far given. The kind of knowledge the society disseminates results in a keener and wider appreciation of the special problems and background of people living in the several distinct regions of this extensive country. In all that it does the society makes for greater mutual understanding among all Canadians, and to this extent is an invaluable agency in creating and promoting greater national unity.

We do operate one Canso aeroplane for aerial magnetic surveys under the geological survey, and that Canso plane is also equipped with a radioactivity detector instrument. It has been found by experience that what they call drift will distort the radioactivity of a region. In other words, it provides a shielding effect and the result is that while radioactive areas are indicated they are not able from the results to locate with certainty where the major deposits are. They have found it useful in relation to their geological mapping. It is useful in identifying the rocks. So far we have not published these reports because we believe they are rather misleading to anyone but an expert, but to a limited degree they are useful in studying and identifying the various rocks of a region.
The hon. member for St. Paul's wanted to know about the distribution of our reports. The reports of aerial magnetic surveys usually are not released for about a year or two after the survey is made, for the simple reason that it takes a great deal of time to compile the results on topographical maps. A mailing list is built up in the meantime, and the public is informed that the map will be released on a certain date. No one has an advantage. It is made available to all comers at the same time.
Others have made reference to the distribution of our maps and reports. The printing bureau sends out notices from time to time, usually by postcard, of new reports that are ready for distribution. Our budget this year for the printing of reports is $216,000, and I believe the printing bureau also has a considerable item for the same purpose. The suggestion of the hon. member for Timis-kaming that these reports be made available to libraries is good. Any library board wishing
